**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Economics 3 (0725), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2024. Duration: One Hour Forty Five Minutes.**

INSTRUCTIONS TO CANDIDATES: Answer ANY THREE questions. All questions carry equal marks. You are advised to spend the first fifteen minutes reading the paper. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. Calculators are allowed.
enonce_intro_markdown:
Table 2 below shows some population statistics for a hypothetical economy. Study the table carefully and answer the questions that follow:

**Table 2**

| Periods | Total Population | % population aged 0-14 | % population aged 65+ | Live births per year | Deaths per year | Dependency ratio | Population growth rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2000 - 2005 | 17,554,000 | 41.6 | 3.5 | 632,000 | 243,000 | | |
| 2005 - 2010 | 19,599,000 | 40.6 | 3.5 | 691,000 | 270,000 | | |

Le corrigé retient (moins de 15 ans + 65 ans et plus) / (15 à 64 ans) x 100 (82,15 % et 78,89 %) et le taux d'accroissement naturel (naissances - décès) / population x 100 par an (2,22 % et 2,15 %), migrations ignorées ; recalculés par script. À titre de contrôle, la variation de la population entre les deux lignes (11,65 % sur cinq ans) correspond à environ 2,23 % par an, valeur voisine.

Question 4 : le tableau imprimé porte des cases vides pour « Dependency ratio » et « Population growth rate » (recopiées vides dans l'énoncé, remplies dans le corrigé). Points imprimés : (a) 4 + 4, (b) 4, (c) 2, (d) 4, (e) 2, soit 20.

La règle « Answer ANY THREE questions » est exprimée par `regles_choix` (3 sur 5, portée PAPER 3) ; la page de garde ne dit pas combien de questions figurent au sujet, le « 5 » est le nombre de questions imprimées (1 à 5). Aucun total de points n'est imprimé par question (« All questions carry equal marks ») : `points` de l'exercice est laissé vide ; les points de chaque sous-question sont la somme des points imprimés de ses parties ; la somme des points imprimés de chaque question vaut 20.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Complete the table above. (4 marks)

(ii) From the dependency ratio, what conclusion can be made about the standard of living ? (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Completing the table.**

*Dependency ratio* = (young dependants + old dependants) as a percentage of the working-age population (15 to 64 years):

$$
\text{Dependency ratio} = \frac{\%\ \text{aged } 0\text{-}14 + \%\ \text{aged } 65+}{100 - (\%\ \text{aged } 0\text{-}14 + \%\ \text{aged } 65+)} \times 100
$$

- 2000 - 2005: dependants $= 41.6 + 3.5 = 45.1\%$; working-age $= 100 - 45.1 = 54.9\%$; ratio $= \dfrac{45.1}{54.9} \times 100 = 82.15\%$ (about 82 dependants per 100 workers).
- 2005 - 2010: dependants $= 40.6 + 3.5 = 44.1\%$; working-age $= 100 - 44.1 = 55.9\%$; ratio $= \dfrac{44.1}{55.9} \times 100 = 78.89\%$ (about 79 dependants per 100 workers).

*Population growth rate* (natural rate of increase, per year) $= \dfrac{\text{births} - \text{deaths}}{\text{total population}} \times 100$:

- 2000 - 2005: $\dfrac{632\,000 - 243\,000}{17\,554\,000} \times 100 = \dfrac{389\,000}{17\,554\,000} \times 100 = 2.22\%$
- 2005 - 2010: $\dfrac{691\,000 - 270\,000}{19\,599\,000} \times 100 = \dfrac{421\,000}{19\,599\,000} \times 100 = 2.15\%$

| Periods | Total Population | % aged 0-14 | % aged 65+ | Live births per year | Deaths per year | Dependency ratio | Population growth rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2000 - 2005 | 17,554,000 | 41.6 | 3.5 | 632,000 | 243,000 | **82.15%** | **2.22%** |
| 2005 - 2010 | 19,599,000 | 40.6 | 3.5 | 691,000 | 270,000 | **78.89%** | **2.15%** |

**(ii) Conclusion about the standard of living.** The dependency ratio **fell from about 82% to about 79%**, so each 100 people of working age support fewer dependants (children and old people). The burden on the working population is lighter, so more income per head is available for consumption, saving and investment, and the government can spend more per child and per old person on health and education. The natural rate of increase also fell slightly (2.22% to 2.15%). The conclusion is that **the standard of living of the people is likely to have improved slightly** between the two periods.

questions.enonce_markdown: State two reasons why the conclusion in 'a (ii)' above may be wrong. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The conclusion may be wrong for the following reasons (any two, 2 marks each):

1. **The dependency ratio is based on age only, not on actual employment.** It assumes that everyone aged 15 to 64 works and everyone else does not. In reality many people of working age are unemployed, in school, housewives or in low-productivity informal activities, while some children and old people do work (for example on family farms), so the true economic burden may differ.
2. **The standard of living depends on real income per head, not on the age structure alone.** If real national output grows more slowly than the population, if prices rise faster than incomes (inflation), or if income is very unequally distributed, living standards may fall even though the dependency ratio falls. The quality of health, education and public services also matters.
3. The figures are averages for hypothetical periods and say nothing about regional differences or about changes within each period.

questions.enonce_markdown: Apart from the evidence in the table above, state one other factor that may affect the actual population growth rate. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown: **Net migration**, that is immigration minus emigration. The table gives only the natural increase (births minus deaths). If more people enter the country than leave (for example refugees or foreign workers), the actual growth rate is higher than the natural rate; if many people emigrate in search of jobs, it is lower. (Wars, epidemics or famine, which raise the death rate, are other examples.)

questions.enonce_markdown: Outline four benefits of an increase in the size of population. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
An increase in the size of a population can bring the following benefits (any four, 1 mark each):

1. **A larger labour force**: more workers are available to produce goods and services, so potential output and economic growth rise, provided jobs exist.
2. **A larger domestic market**: more consumers raise demand, which allows firms to produce on a larger scale and enjoy economies of scale and lower unit costs.
3. **Greater division of labour and specialisation**, which raises productivity.
4. **More investment and entrepreneurship**: a bigger market and a bigger pool of talent encourage new businesses, innovation and the use of idle resources.
5. **A larger tax base**: more taxpayers give the government more revenue for infrastructure and social services.
6. **A younger population** replaces ageing workers and reduces the future burden of old-age dependency.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which economic theory did Rev. Thomas Malthus base his population theory on ? (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown: Malthus based his population theory on the **law of diminishing returns** (diminishing marginal returns applied to land, a fixed factor). He argued that population tends to grow in a **geometric progression** (1, 2, 4, 8, ...) while food production, because land is limited and more labour on the same land yields less and less extra output, grows only in an **arithmetic progression** (1, 2, 3, 4, ...). Population would therefore outrun food supply unless checked by preventive checks (late marriage) or positive checks (famine, disease, war).
